title: Beyond Magnitude: Scale-Invariant Evidential Fusion for Multi-View Classification
claim: Existing fusion rules swing between false confidence and performance collapse as input scale changes, while ours stays flat across all scales.
layout: 2 vertically stacked line plots, shared log x-axis, shaded zones with arrow callouts
description: Two vertically stacked line plots share a log-scale x-axis, the scale factor T, running from 10^-2 to 10^2. The top panel plots accuracy (%). A red dashed line with circle markers, labeled Baselines (DS, Sum, Mean, Weighted), rises slightly near 49%, then falls to about 24% at large T. A pink band shows its variance. A flat blue line with square markers, labeled Ours (Scale-Invariant), stays at about 48%. The right half is shaded gray and labeled Suppression Zone (Performance Collapse). Red arrows mark Accidental Success and Collapse. The bottom panel plots uncertainty (vacuity). The red baseline with triangle markers climbs from about 0.14 to about 0.53, while the blue line with diamond markers stays flat at about 0.4. The left half is shaded gray and labeled Amplification Zone (False Confidence). A red arrow marks False Confidence (Uncertainty → 0). The eye goes first to the diverging red curve and the flat blue line.

abstract: Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) enables trustworthy multi-view classification, yet suffers from a critical vulnerability: the Scale Mismatch Problem. We theoretically demonstrate that existing evidential fusion rules erroneously equate logit magnitude with semantic confidence, rendering them susceptible to semantic hijacking by inflated but uninformative views. To resolve this, we propose Scale-Invariant Evidential Fusion (SAEF), a framework utilizing instance-wise standardization to strictly decouple confidence from scale. Instead of relying on magnitude dominance, SAEF aggregates views based on statistical consensus. Theoretically, SAEF guarantees invariance to global scaling and robustness to asymmetric dominance. Experiments on four diverse datasets confirm that SAEF outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in accuracy and robustness to semantic conflicts and noise, ensuring stability against severe scale perturbations.
